question: What is the main reason we remove stitches (sutures) once a wound has healed?

options.A: Eliminating foreign material once the wound is closed
options.B: Reducing the systemic temperature of the recovering patient
options.C: Preventing the total breakdown of the subcutaneous fat layer
options.D: Stimulating rapid collagen production in the deep tissue

explanation: You're doing great! Stitches are foreign objects to the body. Once the skin has closed up and can hold itself together, taking them out stops irritation and keeps scarring down. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h1)

question: A patient asks why stitches must come out if the wound looks completely closed. What is your best response?

options.A: Fresh air is required underneath the thread to complete deep healing
options.B: Unremoved threads will immediately trigger a severe systemic infection
options.C: The body will naturally dissolve the nylon material over the next month
options.D: Leaving them in too long causes permanent skin marks and inflammation

explanation: Spot on! If stitches stay in too long, the skin grows around them, leaving ugly marks (often called railroad tracks) and causing unnecessary irritation. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why are facial stitches usually removed earlier than stitches on the leg?

options.A: Less exposure to environmental dust and bacteria
options.B: Thicker skin layers that absorb the thread material
options.C: Fewer nerve endings that register pulling sensations
options.D: A richer blood supply and faster healing rate

explanation: Think of the face as having a fantastic blood supply! That extra oxygen and rich blood help facial tissues heal much faster than other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h2)

question: A patient with a cut on their shin asks why their stitches need to stay in for three weeks. How do you explain it?

options.A: Skin on the leg is much thinner and tears easily during pulling
options.B: Lower extremities have slower healing and experience higher movement tension
options.C: The shinbone must be completely calcified before threads come out
options.D: Leg tissue requires extra time to dissolve the metal staples inside

explanation: You've got this! Legs have to deal with gravity and a lot of movement, plus they don't heal quite as fast as the face, so those stitches need a bit more time to do their job. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which of these is a clear sign that you should STOP removing stitches?

options.A: Incomplete wound closure with gaping edges
options.B: Small scabs forming directly over the thread entry points
options.C: Light pink skin along the immediate incision line
options.D: Mild itching reported by the patient near the knot

explanation: Safety first! If the edges of the wound are still gaping open, the skin isn't ready yet. Leave the remaining stitches in so the wound doesn't pop back open. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h3)

question: What is the main danger of taking out stitches from a wound that hasn't healed properly?

options.A: Permanent discoloration of the surrounding epidermis
options.B: Immediate systemic shock from localized blood loss
options.C: Rapid overgrowth of scar tissue over the incision
options.D: Complete wound dehiscence and tissue separation

explanation: Dehiscence just means the wound pops open! Without the stitches holding it together, normal body movement can cause the weak healing tissue to split apart again. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h3)

question: What special feature makes suture scissors different from regular medical scissors?

options.A: A built-in magnifying glass for inspecting tiny knots
options.B: A small curved notch on one blade to slide under the thread
options.C: Extra-long handles for reaching deep surgical cavities
options.D: Serrated edges designed to cut through metal surgical wire

explanation: That little notch on the blade is a lifesaver! It acts like a tiny hook that holds the thread steady so it doesn't slip while you're cutting. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h4)

question: Why is it important to gather all your equipment before you start removing stitches?

options.A: To maintain a sterile field and prevent leaving the patient unattended
options.B: To comply with federal regulations regarding surgical instruments
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of discarded gauze and packaging
options.D: To ensure the doctor is present during the entire process

explanation: Getting everything ready beforehand means you won't have to scramble or leave your patient's side, helping you keep the area clean and safe. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h4)

question: Why must you cut the stitch right next to the skin before pulling it out?

options.A: To ensure the knot stays attached to the forceps for counting
options.B: To avoid dragging the exposed, contaminated thread through the tissue
options.C: To prevent the patient from feeling any pulling sensation
options.D: To save extra suture material for future dressing changes

explanation: Smart nursing! The part of the thread sitting outside the skin has touched the air and picked up bacteria. If you pull that dirty part *through* the skin, you can cause an infection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h5)

question: You are removing stitches from an abdominal wound. After lifting the knot gently with your forceps, what is your next step?

options.A: Apply adhesive remover to dissolve the knot before cutting
options.B: Scrape the skin around the thread with a sterile scalpel blade
options.C: Slide the scissors under the thread close to the skin and snip
options.D: Pull the knot firmly straight up until the entire stitch pops out

explanation: You've got the technique down! Lifting the knot gives you space to slip your scissors underneath close to the skin, making it easy to snip just one side and pull the thread out smoothly. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h5)

question: What instruction should you give a patient after removing their stitches?

options.A: Soak the area in warm bathwater immediately to loosen scabs
options.B: Keep the wound clean and dry for at least 24 to 48 hours
options.C: Scrub the incision daily with harsh antibacterial soap and a brush
options.D: Apply heavy petroleum jelly over the open tracks every hour

explanation: Giving clear home care is key. Keeping the area dry for a day or two lets those tiny little holes where the stitches were close up safely without bacteria getting in. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h6)

question: Why do nurses sometimes place sterile adhesive strips (steri-strips) across a wound right after removing the stitches?

options.A: To seal out all oxygen so the skin cells can multiply faster
options.B: To deliver topical antibiotics directly into the fat layers
options.C: To cover up unsightly scarring left by the surgical needles
options.D: To provide extra mechanical support while tensile strength increases

explanation: Think of steri-strips as a helpful little hug for the skin! They hold the edges together and take the strain off the fresh scar while it continues to get stronger. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h6)

question: What usually happens if a small piece of a stitch is accidentally left behind inside the skin?

options.A: Chronic inflammation and foreign body reaction
options.B: Complete numbness of the surrounding epidermis
options.C: Instantaneous healing of the deep muscle tissue
options.D: Rapid dissolution of the nearby bone structure

explanation: The body treats any leftover thread like an unwelcome guest! It fights back with an immune response, leading to swelling, soreness, and sometimes a stubborn little infection. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h7)

question: How can you as a nurse make sure you don't leave a broken stitch fragment behind?

options.A: Pull all threads out rapidly without checking their length
options.B: Flush the wound with high-pressure hydrogen peroxide to dissolve nylon
options.C: Inspect the wound with an X-ray machine before starting the procedure
options.D: Count every removed piece and match it to the original suture record

explanation: Always count your pieces! Matching what you take out against the medical chart ensures you leave nothing behind in the patient's skin. Excellent clinical habit! [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h7)
